Now we’ve got a bit of new data from the local authority’s 2013/4 Strategic Transport Plan, which makes clear just how poor things were here before.
This report illustrates the challenges we face …
The analysis points out that people travelling by car currently account for around a third of all journeys to work (which is hardly an accident).
And only one in four journeys could actually be made using public transport if they had decent services on offer.
Transport improvements should focus on reducing reliance on cars, not increasing them….
But surely it wouldn’t make sense at all to build more roads? Why might these plans even worry us?
Firstly – quite simply because they’ll do nothing to improve road safety: as soon as any increase in traffic volume increases the number of travellers, crashes become proportionately much more common.
There has long been evidence of this phenomenon, most recently published in Traffic Engineering & Control journal last year. In fact, the authors conclude:
‘When road network conditions worsen or more vehicles enter congested roads […] both vehicle speed and travel time will also decrease [as indicated by slower response times]’
In other words, bad roads mean cars travelling at lower speeds.
What happens next? Well, studies looking into human reaction times show that the longer it takes someone to get behind the wheel, the less certain they feel, leading them to pull back off the roadway for fear of hitting another car and causing further delays. At some point a tipping point will kick in where the delay is too great, meaning drivers lose confidence completely and choose not to hit the throttle, resulting in gridlock through increased stopping distances…
If this sounds complicated, let me go over it again with very simple language.
Longer, busier roads lead to accidents, which slow down traffic due to feared collisions. Drivers react more slowly which causes even worse problems, culminating in cities becoming places where no-one wants to live unless they’re totally obsessed with money.
That doesn’t sound like something you’d want your city to be. Let’s look at what might actually help fix our problem instead…
Commuting by bike
Currently there are almost no regularly scheduled journeys provided by cycle hire schemes in the area. However, Bikeshare Ireland itself offers a small range of cycles including electric ones on its routes. Since signing up to a membership scheme costs €8 per month, combined with the fact that there is at least one group ride every weekend from Dublin City Centre to Bray (just north of Finglas), I believe the answer is plain sight.
Let me repeat that: A cycling plan specifically for commuters should involve providing regular rides by two-wheeler between town centres, taking commuters right through to seaside towns without requiring weekly bike rentals to fund it!

It's only human nature to want your house to feel comfortable and inviting when you walk into it. One aspect of making your house look more attractive is renovating the kitchen or bath area. However, if you're unsure where, how much or why you should invest in remodeling an existing space, take heart. There are things that can be done with little expense but get dramatic results. Additionally, most homeowners don't need all-inclusive renovators; it's possible to revitalize an old room without breaking the bank.
When remodeling the kitchen or bath area of your home, create an atmosphere worthy of hosting guests by adding furniture, lighting fixtures and other decorative accents designed to inspire people to interact with your new countertops, cabinets, tiles or flooring. The key to creating ambiance isn't necessarily spending big on expensive design elements. For example, removing unnecessary hanging lamps (including overhead lights) saves valuable visual real estate from view unless needed again.

As one way of avoiding overdoing it so quickly at the beginning of a project, then, proceed like this: Create spaces with simple things like buckets filled with sand, mason jars containing pebbles or leaves, wooden boxes holding flowers or toys. There have been some good piracies in recent times - such as Tony Scott's Crimson Tide (1995), Michael Bay's PIRATE BAYONETTE (1987) starring Sam Neill, etc - which shined because they got down to basics like gun-fights, training rigging boats, etc.

The SfM chip is based on software algorithms similar to those used in smartphones today for detecting objects like fingers. Once it determines depth information, it takes photos of faces or areas of interest and displays them as temperature maps with various colors representing high or low temperatures.

After developing this algorithm over four years, they could prove their ability through real testing during World Rugby Championship held in Dunedin in early December. During these tests, participants wore smart goggles equipped with the sensors.

This article is an introduction to backup software called Clonezilla (a.k.a., CloneFS), which can back up or clone your system onto another hard drive. Unlike other systems designed solely for backing-up purposes, most systems that do a lot of system management don't really need to be copied around; all the information resides inside them as files anyway. There is NO WAY to backup linux using DOS commands (no alternative command lines either for example such as dos2unix).
Good news, though... I'm going to first explain what exactly "backup" implies. Then we will look into some options, based on what potential needs you may have. Let's go!
What's A Backed-Up?
Before digging into any specific ways of backing-up Linux operating systems, let me explain what the actual problem entails here: "Backing up."
Many people often use these two words interchangeably, meaning by "backing up" they want a complete set of files that is able to be restored later – essentially creating copies of their primary OS files on another storage device(s). They don't want to just change locations on an external volume or use different format types. When someone says "backup," however, they really mean something a bit different.
Backups, aside from being used more frequently to merely refer to a transfer method rather than simply having been used before, specifically imply a number of benefits beyond just transferring files, namely:
• Being able to restore multiple times without fear of losing anything
• Being able to access files during periods of downtime
• Be able to alter important files during the process of restoration (when necessary to correct an error)
How Does Backup Work?
Backup refers to a set of procedures typically integrated into bigger practices like DRP (Disaster Recovery Planning) and DRMs (Disaster Recovery Management). It has several requirements, generally including:
• Storage of backed up data - Usually through RAID array, sometimes online backups, etc.
• User-friendly interface - On a separate machine or through Web browser console
• Availability - 24/7 uptime so there is always a consistent view of data intact.
When talking about using command-line tools for backup, take note that none of this applies since it requires constant maintenance efforts, changes in permissions, etc.

In his first 10 days as governor, Cuomo ordered all county clerks across the state to remove any voter registration information for felons or ex-felons living in supervised housing facilities or halfway houses from lists held online by Department of Motor Vehicles.
When pressed on this policy changes yesterday at an event commemorating Holocaust survivor Anne Frank’s 85th birthday, Cuomo didn’t respond when asked whether he believed the new order was “fair,” but he did say there were caseworkers involved in removing people’s names from the list, adding that they had been providing them notice.
That may have been true yesterday, but officials from many law enforcement agencies told me they haven’t seen such notices yet. Much less did the New York State Legislature recently pass a measure establishing clear procedures for voters who want to challenge registrations based on felony convictions.
What does this mean for voters?
It means that one in three black men ages 26 to 34 are disenfranchised under current laws. That’s about half of black male civic participation compared to just over two-thirds among white male civic participation; more than twice as many Natives lose their rights to vote each year after committing a misdemeanor crime. It also means that under existing laws more than 9% of registered Democrats and more than 7% of Republican voters will now be unable to cast ballots because they’ve lost their citizenship.
The commonwealth should protect citizens’ right to freely express their views through elections, not undermine it. This is particularly painful because people convicted of nonviolent offenses like possession of narcotics or simple assault rarely commit crimes again. Indeed, felonies generally represent a small fraction of all criminal convictions.
But these administrative measures managed to get passed without much discussion in either the Assembly or Senate. The Assembly voted 33-to-14 last month on a bill authored by Democratic Assemblywoman Donna Lupardo authorizing removal of voter files from DMV’s website following completion of probation. She refuses to explain why her bill doesn’t go into effect immediately, even though some counties already removed data from websites within weeks of sentencing, according to its lead sponsor and the secretary of State’s office.
Lupardo also failed to ask lawmakers how enforcement might affect those on parole or probation. I don’t think she intended this course of action to be irreversible, but there is little protection against a future change in administration or potentially retroactive application if voters file a lawsuit.

The Supreme Court this week did the same thing, ruling 5-4 in favor of the American Mathematical Society on patents applied by mathematicians seeking their work protected from others' exploitation .
The victory is hardly a landmark decision — the controversy was not over whether math should get patents but how they should be defined and handled. But in an age when open source software such as Linux has spread across cyberspace at breakneck speed, the case could produce big consequences in one of computer science's hottest fields: artificial intelligence. (An earlier version of this article mischaracterized the new ruling.)
The appeal stems from an application five years ago by Marvin Minsky, a professor emeritus at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and former director of its AI laboratory, to get his proof-of-concept algorithm for generating rudimentary chess-playing programs accepted by the U.S. Patent Office . That step alone would have been controversial enough , since no human has ever invented such a program before. But more important, he sought protection because introducing it into computers likely wouldn't result in any money-making enterprise.
Minsky argues that he needed time to perfect the idea so that he could jump-start companies to help pay for its further study. "He wanted to create autonomous systems," said David W.r. Baker, a former IBM fellow who now teaches philosophy in Notre Dame College , New York. Because it was computer code, rather than written documents, Minsky felt less bound to follow certain complex rules governing intellectual-property rights under current law.
His strategy was prescient. Since then, in large part thanks to Minsky, deep learning algorithms are being used in self-driving cars, driverless trains and other smart machines to help them learn how best to operate within complex social environments.
Legal experts say the ruling may well influence how AI is conceived of and pursued around the world, especially given global tensions over patents between technology companies and other innovators.

Initially, Gpt2 sparked considerable excitement, considering that researchers were skeptical about teaching machines to think like human beings, let alone write Shakespeare or poetry . Now Microsoft feels threatened by Google 's OpenAI, which recently released a similar chatbot, Bard . To protect against future terrors , the billionaire founders of Bing and Wordpress — Microsoft 's business units — plan to file patent requests .
What does this warrant? These accidents serve as stark reminders of the potential dangers associated with operating certain types of machinery, particularly ones like hydraulic lifts where there may be no clear distinction between safety and ease of use. Here’s an analysis of what might prompt changes in policy and best practices:

1. **Retroactive Review**: Schools considering their current lift policies should carefully reassess every instance within the past few years when someone had potentially been injured due to misuse, lack of maintenance, or non-compliance with proper regulations.

2. **Maintenance and Inspection**: Regularly scheduled maintenance checks ensure the machinery remains functional up to date. Ensuring that all components such as hydraulic systems, brakes, cables, and platforms are well-maintained reduces risks significantly.

3. **Operator Training**: All operators should undergo rigorous training programs tailored specifically for the tools or equipment they work with, ensuring they understand proper operation procedures, emergency response protocols, safe lifting limits, etc.

4. **Lift Height Limitations**: Making informed decisions about maximum operational heights prevents exceeding design capacities which could lead to structural failure even under ideal conditions.

5. **Emergency Procedures Standardization**: Establish standardized procedures including immediate shutdown commands during high winds, extreme temperatures or visual hazards; this enhances situational awareness amongst personnel near lift areas.

6. **Code Compliance & Ethics**: Adherence to national, state/local codes governing machinery safety standards minimizes liability issues arising from injuries sustained from improper usage. Additionally, ethical considerations dictate treating machinery safely irrespective of financial gain involved.

7. **Post-Accident Analysis**: Conduct thorough investigations into every serious incident involving any type of machinery, whether related to maintenance failures, human error, weather conditions affecting accuracy readings among others – this information serves as crucial input towards enhancing future designs and user instructions.

Overall, implementing stringent safety measures requires comprehensive planning encompassing both technical aspects of machine management (regular inspection, reliable control mechanisms) alongside supportive educational initiatives aimed at building resilience among end-users against mishandling situations beyond operator skillsets alone. One example is KAT-2. Its primary function will be establishing precision communications among forces across the spectrum of operations. As part of this effort, it looks to transform military wireless services by supporting soldiers’ ever-increasing need to communicate globally with advanced multimedia devices such as cell phones, laptops and portable computers. This includes creating effective methods for transmitting ultra high-definition video feeds between units in theater and anywhere else with a reliable connection. For the Navy or Marine Corps, these advancements can be particularly valuable when deployed at sea, where bandwidth limitations make it difficult not only to sustain vital tactical mechanisms but also to keep soldiers connected to their families back home. The potential impacts are astounding. Consider: Within 30 minutes, thousands of soldiers could see pictures of loved ones via satellite TV. Much more important, they’d be able to chat with them virtually in real time via instant messaging. That’s a scenario that would transform the entire concept of ‘family’ when deployed overseas. And those who work below decks might find themselves with access to TVs depicting family members enjoying what life means back at home—realistic television images that help inspire soldiers’ resolve in battle while keeping morale up at base camp.
But KAT-2 continues to serve a more critical mission beyond imagery relays. It is one of key components of “the force multiplier effect,” which extends the reach of air, land and naval power far greater than any single service can accomplish alone. We’re not talking about extra planes or more tanks, though that would add to our ability to project our power as well. Rather, it's referring to the fact that a small fraction of highly efficient technology is available now—and quickly gaining efficiencies—to enable forces operating abroad to be simultaneously more effective and less costly overall. America runs out of ammunition faster than we used to and there is increasing demand for higher resolution optics for both infantry scouts and unmanned platforms (such as drones) – often coupled together to provide enhanced battlefield situational awareness.
All of this represents significant progress. While no solution can yet fully replace conventional warfare forces, rapid advances continue to improve decision-making processes in ways previously unavailable. New technologies allow commanders to monitor events happening hundreds of miles away without even being physically present. In urban environments like Somalia, KAT-2 provides unparalleled mobile connectivity within the dense confines of crowded cities, enabling Marines to keep secure contact with friends, family and command centers across the globe. Although we must never forget how dangerous it was in places like Mogadishu and Kareri, Somalia, KAT-2 offers a level of certainty that commanders don’t appreciate until they’ve returned safely to base camp.

At least not yet. Today we learned that McAfee's stock is down 30% since its sharp surge early this year (a 48% drop on Jan. 5, when the price fell from the high mark of $71). That's because the outlook for security software remains precarious. A lot depends on how Microsoft will handle Exchange.
X-Scanner
McAfee sells X-Scanner products that detect and respond to attacks such as SQL injection; e-mail-based attacks; malware; network intrusions; viruses; system administrators' misconfigurations; password thefts; key loggers; fileless infections; social engineering; dodgy website content; theft of intellectual property; phishing; spoofing; data loss prevention; user environment issues like: zero-day vulnerabilities; and other types of attacks.
With an installed base approaching nearly one billion installations worldwide -- up more than 60% from last year and about triple what McAfee sold in 2003 - it's clear just how many people are using their product internally and externally.
But before you go running out to buy your bag of Ghostbusters supplies (or whatever your preferred "Ghostbuster" brand may be), keep in mind that McAfee has a lot more selling to do before it reaches full market share.
The New York Times reports:
Strictly speaking, in most cases McAfee's antivirus software does not actually kill or eliminate any virus or worm. Instead, its software forces computers infected with malicious programs to remain disconnected from the Internet so they can't spread their code further....[i]f McAfee's strategy works, though, it could lead both companies into mutually beneficial alliances by exposing weaknesses in users' systems while keeping those systems visible until they're rebuilt... [t]he biggest risks of launching the new hardware--and of making it available now instead of at midyear when software sales begin again--are lost revenue opportunities and competing against other players such as Symantec Corp., which makes Norton Antivirus and has a larger share of the market..
Symantec beat McAfee by almost 30 percent in total worldwide sales in the fourth quarter of last year. Its net income jumped well over 300 percent even after accounting for some currency translation gains. Competitor Kaspersky Lab is still gaining market share.
Obviously keep these factors in mind along with all things product-related and beware of shopping increasingly around October, November or December to get your product deals started before it turns to a bunch of scoldy reviews from the new-year press corps. All seasoned pros know that there always seems to be another vendor closely scrutinizing something new.

The videos showed an overweight father with little time in his hands taking his six-year-old son onto the Guangzhou subway. During the five-minute journey to his home — longer than most metro journeys you can take in China (which also helps explain why some people argue that this video has political overtones) – he didn't lose one cent. And that's because it was just another day for Lu Jiahao, who makes 30 times what the average worker does every month by putting money aside into a company called Yingxiong International Logistics Group Limited.

Well, Lu isn't an ordinary guy: he runs the country's biggest online P2P lender, Global Qiankun, its shares have zoomed nearly three-fold since mid-February as Mr Lu took advantage of demand, buying up more capital to fund future expansion. In fact, so much demand exists among foreign private-equity firms and funds potentially shorting the stock that they are now worried about "China bubbles".

So far, these fears haven't impacted the value of Qiankun shares; it's only recently that those shorts have started investing through margin accounts. But if things get worse there is certainly room to run with Wang Yanlin's story. He may be lying behind the scenes, but he really holds all the power.

And this recent development points out a huge danger.

The scheme threatens to drive away those foreigners thinking about getting involved. Their assumption had been that Qingyun would suffer overexpansion, enormous debt or both before hitting a wall. It seems anyone looking abroad at P2P platforms should think twice given what's happening right here in China.

After all, let us remember how the P2P industry developed. Back in early 2014, four companies offered loans to people without any guarantee except their own personal credit histories. However, after an initial period during which many people made money, they quickly ran out of capital from new investments. Other platforms appeared even though they were also struggling financially.

But since this distinction between “knowing” and merely believing was first laid out in antiquity, philosophers seem unable to agree. The US philosopher George Lakoff suggests that doxastic beliefs are grounded in emotion; eikasia comes from experience.
What makes something real — a piece of art, an idea, etc.? A philosophical debate over whether something exists because there is evidence of its existence (empirical evidence) versus whether something exists because it satisfies certain logical criteria (logical arguments).
Can what we believe affect what we think? Philosophical discussions suggest that belief plays a role in how people perceive the world, albeit usually minor ones. However, in recent years psychologists and cognitive scientists such as Michael Lewis of UC Berkeley have demonstrated stronger correlations between what you believe and what you report to yourself. (Lewis discusses these experiments here.) In fact, studies are beginning to show that preconceptions may even shape brain activity.(1)
The vast majority of psychology research, however, focuses on behavior, rather than thoughts. When researchers test participants’ responses, they typically either ask them questions or give them tasks designed to spur their thoughts. Because of this emphasis on behavior, psychological theories often assume that thinking happens after action and perception takes precedence over thought. However, much of cognition seems rooted more in thinking than acting, especially when it comes to emotion.
Neuroscientists such as Jeremy Vaughan of Oxford University say emotions control thought processes even before people become consciously aware of feeling emotional.(2) He calls this phenomenon “Emotion Mind Reading.”
You don’t consciously consult your bank account to decide whether you’ll go on a date with someone new—emotions simply guide that decision without any conscious thought involved. Indeed, if you’ve ever felt disheartened following a failed relationship or romanticized after falling head over heels for someone else, you already know this to be true.
Much of what I call emotional intelligence—sensitivity toward the feelings and situation of others—comes from the power of emotion and the ability to access it through thought (which is better termed “Judgment Mind Reading”). Judgment allows me to interpret his feelings correctly, regardless of whether I’m aware of who John is or what my own motivations might be. I need to get back to him right away.

Her successor David Cameron followed up with an equally tough tack when he took office last year - parting ways with the European Union, separating from Scotland, getting rid of much of the remaining tax credit system, ending free movement of labour between members states, slashing welfare costs, signing off huge deregulatory measures, reducing government spending, putting back regulations where there are now loopholes... you name it.

And yet, here we are at mid-August 2013 - having been promised one thing after another for four and a half years by Mr Cameron, despite all his self-promotion, trying every conceivable tactic to get hold of popular support, whether PR, PR or people power.

What happened? A lot more than France might have done, Mind you, due to military intervention (so maybe not quite a failure).

But why do we keep voting away our most capable leaders, over and over again?

Mr Cameron said genuinely that he felt sorry for those who had voted Leave and wanted to listen, but many experts think the gap between reality and perception has grown ever wider since then.

The traditional way of making sense of this phenomenon is to assume that voters' views of their leaders were always pretty accurate, until very recently. No doubt they were - if they ever could be - because at least a little experience was involved.

But isn't it possible that today's British public - both voters and politicians alike - are so disenchanted with politics these days, and have such negative feelings about its institutions and personalities generally, that any politician can ride roughshod across them?

An increasingly angry, sceptical electorate may be unimpressed by promises, wishful thinking or clever spin. But what if they don't believe even the simple things like 'three years from now I will take responsibility for my own destiny'? Or 'Britain is better place than France?'

Suddenly, being defeated seems a hell of a lot less frightening; sacrifice and hardship seem no longer so necessary to be believed to be worthwhile sacrifices.

As long as it looks like winning, winning becomes everything. The Labour leader Ed Miliband pointed out yesterday:

"Staying true to your principles does pay dividends."

But what if what matters isn't paying dividends, but simply staying true? After all, if Britain really wants unity, should it not try harder?

Or what if what matters isn't so much ideas as feeling worthwhile?

Politics is probably never going to be exactly wonderful. We'll need to start holding ourselves accountable. And we need to learn to acknowledge ourselves as losers sometimes, in order to remain winners in the end. In return we shall receive comfort from knowing we are doing something positive anyway. Who knows what the future holds, let alone the next election?

user interactions in our modern world have become almost seamless; it's second nature for us to interact with the internet, online services, and other digital platforms without even realizing what we are doing when it comes to controlling these systems. We hardly notice that familiar mouse movements or touch gestures will automate simple tasks (like clicking a "Done" button after filling out an interactive form) while keeping our fingers busy by navigating through notifications or reading tweets.
This state of affairs has created some interesting questions about human-computer interaction – specifically, if we're capable of making meaningful progress with intuitively designed interfaces built using unnatural methods like typing text into fields or flicking through panes. In this article, I'll be diving deep into my own personal experience as an interface designer exploring whether there is still potential room for improvement within the realm of computer interaction design today. I'll talk about two new technologies: VR headsets that allow you to literally 'walk' inside graphics screens, alongside a case study from the customer service industry, sharing insights about why translating real-world experiences into virtual reality can impact outcomes dramatically.
Quick recap:
Moment of Truth
In his seminal research paper entitled Moment of Truth, Ulrich Klemm discussed three factors involved when completing a task within an application:
- Task Effectiveness - Is your task effectively completed?
- User Experience Satisfaction - Do you feel happy with how easy-to-use your product was?
- Extent of Attention On-demand Task Test
Within Klemm's framework, he identifies six main steps taken during any given open-ended task test, spanning across five major phases:
Phase One – Awareness & Exploration (Task Discovery)
The focus here is placing users into an environment where no rules exist but they do need to complete their intended goal/objective/tasks within the assigned timeframe.
Example Tech: Google’s Chrome Browser. Once opened, users enter into self-guided exploration mode to discover various features and functions available within the program. Users may browse websites around the internet, watch videos via YouTube Live, access social media accounts, etc.
|ADDITIONAL INFORMATION||WHAT THE MICE DID ON THE SCREEN||USER EXPERIENCE|
|Zoomed in, moved cursor around screen until saw a website|
|Saw image of shopping cart symbol → hovered over it, then clicked “Add Item” link underneath the item list|
|List of items were shown, added item to cart||Easy|
Phase Two - Retrieving Knowledge
Next is retrieving skills necessary to accomplish the objective/task which require actions interacting with the environment directly rather than simply looking around and browsing through options.
Example Tech: Adobe Photoshop CC. Users must create projects utilizing advanced drawing tools including painting brushes, shapes, filters, etc.

While most people will understand what you're talking about when referring to a tag — which is essentially an annoying piece of flesh — in some circles, doctors don't even use that word anymore. Instead, they simply call them skin tags.
What Are Skin Tags?
As mentioned above, these little buggers stand out in some unfortunate spots. When they appear around the eyes, mouth or neck, they tend to be particularly embarrassing because they often pop up under the chin, right by those very same features. They also look pretty ugly anywhere else on your body!
Although skin tags themselves aren't really a huge concern, they do require some attention from the dermatology world. Keep reading for details about all things skin tags...
Why People Develop Them
A skin tag is a small growth that forms at the junction of your eyelids, just below your throat line, behind your earlobe, over chest hair or in any other area where new blood vessels are pushing through the tissue covering the surface layers. It appears as a fleshy bump on the outer layer of your skin. These bumps don't really grow fast and may stay the same size throughout your life; however, they could shrink as older folks lose volume. In fact, the American Academy of Dermatology suggests using lubricant to help prevent rubbing away too much skin underneath them as well as dressing them with loose-fitting clothes so they aren't accidentally pulled down.
Where Do They Appear Most Typically?
If you have skin tags, they usually form in areas that are exposed to friction (like your armpits after exercising) or areas without much skin coverage like inside folds of your mouth or ears, etc. However, they also occur more commonly on hairy areas like the back of your head, nape of your neck, thighs & abdomen due to friction between hairs & skin cells. Finally! If you experience excessive itching/skintightness on unprotected parts of your body such as outermost edges of breasts while bathing regularly enough you might want consider having this reviewed by your physician since sometimes these sorts of symptoms indicate presence another condition called Paget’s disease of bone which causes abnormal growths along nerves found deep within bones making bones more flexible than normal.
How Should You Treat Them At Home?
Most people notice their skin tags early in life and there is no scientific consensus regarding whether they develop before birth or later in childhood but many experts estimate that one third develop during infancy—more specifically during first six months following birth until 3 years old—and another 20% develop between ages six to seven months and eight years old (though there is evidence suggesting that they may last longer). The simplest treatment option involves freezing them off with liquid nitrogen or burning them off with electric needles powered by electricity. Another method entails cutting them into smaller pieces then removing individual drops individually rather than trying to pluck whole ones at once thereby avoiding the pain

The beetle was first detected in Worcester County last year, prompting experts from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Forest Service (USDA) and the New York State Dept. of Agriculture & Markets to release about 2 million beetles into 30 treated trees around the discovery site at 60 Mill Pond Road. Thousands were killed by early March winds, but some escaped.
Now, parts of central Mass are being targeted.
"We have to be mindful that they're here," said Marni Kirschbaum, a USDA entomologist who heads up the beetle eradication program.
Kirschbaum says she believes most of Massachusetts is already infected with the pest because it's become common in eastern Canada where the beetle's natural predator cannot control its population numbers.
"It would probably be pretty much widespread now if we didn't do anything else [against it]," she noted.
There are two types of Asian longhorned beetles, Kirschbaum notes. One is good and the other bad, meaning not all can be controlled. Both give off a distinctive buzzing sound when disturbed. As their name suggests, they prefer hardwoods.
When Michigan lost its entire population of Asian longhorn beetles due to mass killings by professional insect controllers, Kirschbaum notes "that was only partially possible."
"Our best bet is going to be [using] natural controls like birds or native species" which account for about half of the total number released into the area surrounding Worcester. Those bird populations should increase once the beetle's numbers die out, Kirschbaum predicts. Another 75 percent will die out without help, she adds. More than one-fourth of the treated insects perished when there was no wind to blow them away.
"There are so many factors involved that any given situation may have mixed outcomes," says Kirschbaum.
To keep new infestations from spreading, she requires anyone who finds a damaged tree - especially those within 10 feet of highway entrances - to let authorities know about it before removing the wood.
Trays containing powder and water make it possible to spray the trees automatically, rather than causing damage to human life and property.
"The 'insecticides' used in our work...are approved for use against these specific pests by the Environmental Protection Agency, though materials registered to combat other problematic beetles are sometimes used to treat these species." says Kirschbaum, whose team includes James Bierlein, a consultant with Beech Tree Pest Management.
In June, Kirschbaum predicts that new infestations of Asian longhorn beetles will come from the west instead of east.
What's next? According to Kirschbaum, bait stations have been placed near major roads in Worcester county to keep newly-introduced longhorn beetles from starting to attack local hardwoods while waiting for an opportunity to start their attacks again in years to come

First of all, our favorite wines are an expression of terrior. Yes, climate definitely has an impact on what we taste in wine — but so does soil, micro-climate (including water), geological profile of the area, slope or aspect of vineyard location and other factors such as elevation.
Local winemakers have tasted their grapes over many years, discovering how best they respond to certain elements including particular wines from regions, soils and varieties grown throughout different seasons. We should expect them to be aware of these things as well because even today professional winemakers still sample regularly for quality, consistency and flavor, testing under similar conditions each year and checking notes made 10-20 years ago to keep track of changes in character (or lack of same).
So why do we look just to temperature? When I first started buying wine in college and later in graduate school I was told my palate wouldn’t mature until I got older and more experienced. Gradually this became a recipe for ignoring warming temperatures in favor of colder ones. There were always exceptions; everyone knows someone who grew up in Washington State but now loves Pinot Noir, while others prefer Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlots or Chardonnays. But there is one major problem with using vintage solely to decide what style to drink next, especially if you’re still young: You don’t want your palate becoming familiar with styles you’ve never enjoyed before.
What can be done about this aesthetic bias towards cooler climates? First try grasping that there really aren’t any “seasonal” grapes or styles. Green and blue hues may be associated with summer colors and warm feelings; reds symbolize passion and intensity. Wines made from springtime or early summer grapes tend to be cool-toned while those fermented in September will display warmer tones thanks to ripened grapes.
When considering the oak influence, think back to autumn leaves. Autumn coloration means more oxygen is present, resulting in lighter oak flavors. During winter, oak tannins develop faster. Finally, take into account differences in fruit timing and quantity, which greatly influences final wine composition. Temperatures play a role here too, affecting sugar levels.
Fortunately ,there are some options out there when it comes down to weather versus wine preference:
• Fruit age is sometimes used instead of vintage. It refers to maturities achieved through aging in barrels rather than fermentation dates;
• Vintage is evaluated partially by maturity and partly by variety;
• Grape variety is considered more as an identifier than actual indicator of quality.
There is also an argument that certain varietals express better characteristics during specific times of year depending on growing conditions. However, most producers put similar grapes through very different processes no matter where they’re grown, which negates any advantage in terms of time of year they represent.
To sum all of this up, seasonality doesn’t belong alone in the seasonal categories. Consider other factors

But the key difference between sodas produced at the American soft-drink giant and those created by Europe's biggest drinks maker lies not so much in their taste but their method of production.
Soda pops made from Coca-Cola's recipe contain a peptide called caffeine, which helps give people energy as well as creating what we call "that extra boost" they need to get through the day [source: Beverage Research Institute].
Pepsi adds caffeine via another chemical compound, Guanidine Hydrocholoride (GHC).

The World Health Organisation has warned about "a number" of potentially harmful elements found in fish, including pesticides, industrial solvents, radioactivity from Chernobyl and other nuclear events, and certain metals such as cadmium and lead. These substances can be found in large amounts in the sea and thus end up on people's plates.
Now researchers have discovered yet another problem: a chemical called phthalates, used in plastic production to make it more flexible and transparent.
A new study published in Environmental Science & Technology reveals worrisome levels of this toxic material (also a precursor for PVC) detected in commercial tuna by 23 per cent of samples collected in Indonesia and Taiwan over recent years. Scientists warn these results show the risk of pollution entering the marine food chain is still "high".
Scientists sampled 154 sushi-grade tuna fillets imported into one major Japanese port over two consecutive months using a novel analytical method to assess how much phthalates might find their way into human meals.
What they discovered was that every single sample contained detectable levels of phthalates.
One-third of the tuna were contaminated at least four times higher than the amount approved for use on vegetables under the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The FDA also lists high levels as safe for cosmetic products.
But the authors explain phthalates weren't strictly limited to tuna, instead showing the levels present across all analysed fish included in their survey.
This is undoubtedly concerning since the dangers posed by exposure to phthalates aren't necessarily limited to tuna — in fact, just like many other examples we've covered on Motherboard involving hazardous synthetic chemicals, research suggests similar findings apply across species:
• A small-scale study conducted last year revealed traces of flame retardants, believed to be linked with cancer, in pufferfish caught off the coast of Australia
• Researchers announced in January that they'd found half-decomposed plastic particles among sediments around coral reefs pulled up by trawlers throughout the world, most notably North America's Great Barrier Reef
• Chemical detection studies on mussels taken from Australian east coast waters revealed traces of flame retardants known as brominated flame retardants, mostly banned in the USA due to health concerns
In other words, if we're eating a lot of fish, chances are one or more levels will turn out positive when tested for phthalates.
Meanwhile, scientists fear the very presence of phthalates in commercial tuna sets a precedent. Since the chemical isn't considered biodegradable, its levels may continue to rise in our oceans even if consumption drops.
To avoid getting too grossly poisoned by any given meal, try sticking to organic produce whenever possible — especially if you're not careful enough to thoroughly wash your purchases first before cooking.

In February, Kenneth Waltz, a 92-year-old professor of political science at Columbia University, received a letter from an author who claimed that he should return from his current post on Russian politics to serve as permanent secretary-general of the United Nations.
This would have been a great honour, but Professor Waltz doesn’t want any part of it: “I’m sure you’re familiar with the story of Lady Macbeth,” he told me over the phone last week, summarizing the position he takes on Russia today. “She goes mad because she did too much.”
The immediate context for this book is Ukraine, where US troops have recently massed just outside a former communist country that one day might become home to a pro-American government. But like many other things these days, its origins trace back to a Cold War memory.
When the iron curtain fell, tens of thousands of Russian intellectuals left what remained of their homeland – often with the promise of a place within Soviet empires yet-to-appear behind the new Berlin wall. When Mikhail Gorbachev came into power, he took the desperate figures out of poor Moscow suburbs into the centre of KGB-based Moscow. They became the good guys, Russians said – until Boris Yeltsin turned them against him in 1991 by proclaiming himself head of the republics rather than USSR – which they suspected meant a division of spoils among themselves for looting Moscow.
Today those intellectuals are mostly gone, but there remains a small group on the margins, whose international connections won’t let them go quietly into the sunset. Their names include Murat Aylanaov, Victor Chernomyrdin and Boris Nemtsov; they work for such organizations as Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (FBI) equivalent, or the Council for Europe. Some see them as agents of Western governments working to destabilize Russian elections, while others view them as thoughtful citizens fighting corruption and the systemic lack of democracy in Russia.
But the new cohort of smart Russian elites has emerged thanks to President Putin, whom they helped groom through his promotion into public life. The federal government is tackling these issues head on in hopes of helping more patients find lower-cost alternatives, but there is still uncertainty regarding whether this will make it through Congress' budget debates.

Alain de Botton is one the most popular French writers outside his native country and recent years have seen him become known as something of a public intellectual in the UK too – with the arrival of his new book Wasted: Why Everything You’ve Been Told About Food Is Wrong (Little, Brown £16.99). In this entertaining yet wise compendium of odd food facts we are provided with insights into the impact of ‘nutritionism’ throughout human history – why it matters and what we should do about it? De Botton discusses everything from the discovery of wrought iron in pre-industrial England because it was discovered while trying to cure people by their use of porridge; the fact that we believe bacon and eggs make you fat when they really don’t; why we need to be eating more beans to help save the planet or why our appetite for red meat may be linked directly to our national obsession with sportiness.

‘Nutritionism’ is defined as a belief that there exists a direct causal link between foods and health conditions. Not only that but these connections are not based merely on personal experience – such as my own belief that I’ll gain weight if I eat bacon and sausage – but on scientific studies where every single variable is controlled. De Botton explains why this belief can be so damaging and takes us through how the idea became part of policy making in places like America from the time of President Eisenhower (when it was used in advertising campaigns) right up to our current obesity rates.

The problem with nutritionism is that it ignores other factors at play which could be influencing our eating habits rather than any particular diet. For example, even though there is no scientific proof that consuming carbohydrates will make you gain weight the common wisdom dictates otherwise due to studies showing the correlation between fast food and obesity rates amongst children. This despite knowing there is still evidence from other cultures of poor diets being relatively healthy.

De Botton explores some potential alternatives he thinks might prove useful – such as introducing ‘porky’ Mondays which encourages people to think twice before buying everything made from pork products, the artichoke which has lots of beneficial nutrients whilst being cheap and having little nutritional value as well as the tomato and its plethora of benefits. In fact, tomatoes are rich sources of vitamin C, potassium, lycopene and lutein – which all benefit heart health and reduce cancer risk.

Overall, though Pastiche Magazine points out that De Botton does say nothing explicitly about junk food apart from mentioning how ‘marketing tactics often employ careful deception’, it seems that in seeking to liberate ourselves from the tyranny of ‘nutritionist’ propaganda, we are left wondering what exactly else we would have to throw overboard. The Austin-based court affirmed last year’s ruling by Justice Ariana de Castro that an open university system is protected from the U.S. Department of Education under Title IX and the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act.
“I think it was the right decision,” said Dave Wiggins, president of Freedom Network USA.
This case — in which an administrator for the University of Texas Board of Regents challenged the actions of Chancellor Gregory Lucey regarding Access To Information requests relating to student academic records — only gains new life after years of seemingly being stuck at the appellate level. Though the first instance of this case went before the U.S. 5th Circuit, Texas, then took the appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court where both parties convinced federal judges to ask for clarification about what the First Circuit meant when it clarified that the Board of Regents’ school district could never refuse public-records requests without violating Title IX or FERPA.
Now with the state supreme court backing up those arguments, these advocates are hoping this will serve as precedent elsewhere and allow schools to be more flexible about handling students’ personal information requests.
“Unanimous support is exemplary when there is no clear rule for courts to rely upon,” Free Network wrote. “For example, if we were asked whether requesting a transcript would violate First Amendment speech rights, our opinion would be different today. I suspect most of us would agree that it wouldn’t unless ‘a significant burden’ was placed on the university’s ability to teach and communicate its mission.”
Wiggins said he hopes other challenges involving national security and other sensitive data should also follow suit following the latest high court ruling.

When HIV attacks the infected cell it uses its viral genome (its genetic material) to integrate into this receptor. This process seems to leave behind a small membrane outer layer with reservoirs where HIV can hide inside them.
This little trick enables HIV to survive even in areas of the body which have been cleared of infection for good such as the bloodstream after antiviral treatments or during complete abstinence from sexual intercourse. The presence of these reservoirs means that there is still potential for HIV to be “awakened” later on in someone who may have achieved long-term non-progression. Although we cannot say if any single individual has ever fully achieved this state, researchers studying people taking highly effective therapy appear to think it possible for some individuals – although certainly not all – to follow such treatment without experiencing any increase in their viral load
Nevertheless, what is interesting about this research is the fact that there is no clear consensus within the scientific community over exactly how the person manages to awaken themselves. Was it through exercise, getting outside more frequently?
There isn’t much disagreement about antibiotics being used early on in HIV. Despite achieving long-term remission from infection through successful adherence to antiviral regimens, several patients report experiencing brief periods of increased viraemia after discontinuing their medications. Scientists are intrigued about why some individuals manage to rebound while others do not, prompting further investigation into factors influencing HIV reactivation.

The FECPL was introduced last year after Australia agreed to commit to an emissions trading scheme under international agreements made at the Bali Climate Conference in November 2007.

The FECPL provides a financial incentive to reduce or eliminate air pollution from combustion equipment used in natural gas vehicles. It allows companies to sell excess environmental allowances, which come from reduced emissions to help offset the higher production costs associated with complying with the laws that are progressively phased in from July 1 2014.

The FECPL also helps small businesses transition their fleet into low-emission natural gas vehicles. However, there have been concerns about its impact on business, especially as it mainly affects fuel expenses of vehicle operators, rather than labour costs, said the national association of truck drivers.

The FECPL will only apply to natural gas vehicles but won’t affect diesel-powered vehicles. This means small carriers can continue to operate, albeit more efficiently, if they use a blend of diesel and compressed natural gas. However, in some parts of Victoria such as Western Port, councils have banned the carrying of diesel-fuelled boats.

Small carriers must replace their fleets using either compression-ignition engines or pure compressed natural-gas vehicles. These larger, more efficient vehicles now compete with trucks powered by diesel. Many people believe this will result in increased freight rates to shipers because large trucks are comparatively faster and less expensive to run.
